hook: A single galaxy extends across nearly 1.7 million light-years of space.

sections.voiceover: A single galaxy extends across nearly 1.7 million light-years of space.
sections.visual_cue: Deep space view showing an immense glowing elliptical galaxy against dark cosmic void.
b_roll: Deep space astronomical photography of giant elliptical galaxy
sections.animation_cue: Slow push in on central galactic core

sections.voiceover: In 2022, astronomers captured deep space images with the Isaac Newton Telescope. How wide is this giant structure compared to our Milky Way?
sections.visual_cue: Exterior shot of Isaac Newton Telescope dome under starry night sky transitioning to ultra-deep galaxy sky survey data.
b_roll: Isaac Newton Telescope observatory dome timelapse
Astronomy camera digital imaging display showing galactic clusters
sections.animation_cue: Grid overlay scanning across galaxy halo map

sections.voiceover: However, Trujillo's team didn't measure IC 1101 until ultra-deep images revealed its main body.
sections.visual_cue: Astronomical sky survey contour map highlighting extended outer halo of galaxy IC 1101.
sections.animation_cue: Contour line expanding outward from core to faint edge

sections.voiceover: The study determined IC 1101 spans a staggering 520 kiloparsecs. That physical dimension equals nearly 1.7 million light-years across. Astronomy & Astrophysics published these official galactic findings on October 1, 2026.
sections.visual_cue: Graphic scale diagram comparing measured 520 kiloparsec halo diameter against deep space background.
b_roll: Deep space telescope survey frame of IC 1101
Scientific publication diagram overlaying cosmic scale markers
sections.animation_cue: Measurement callout arrows expanding across full frame width

sections.voiceover: IC 1101 remains the largest known galaxy in the Universe.
sections.visual_cue: Wide cinematic pull back showing IC 1101 surrounded by cluster galaxies in distant universe.
sections.animation_cue: Slow continuous zoom out into darkness
